items.t: Waymo restarts San Antonio service 5 months after flooding troubles
items.d: The company suspended service in the city in April after one of its robotaxis got swept away.
items.fullText: In Brief Posted: 11:30 AM PDT · September 17, 2026 Image Credits: Getty Images Sean O'Kane Waymo restarts San Antonio service 5 months after flooding troubles Waymo has restarted its robotaxi service in San Antonio, Texas, five months after one of its vehicles was swept away during a flash flood. Multiple Waymo robotaxis got stuck during the heavy flooding in April. The vehicles slowed but did not stop as they approached waterlogged streets. Waymo ultimately issued a recall in May, and the company restricted its robotaxis from driving in areas with elevated risk of flooding. Waymo briefly paused operations around the same time in other cities in Texas but has since resumed those services. The company is now offering paid rides in 15 U.S. cities. The resumed service in San Antonio will involve dozens of vehicles covering a 60-mile area that includes downtown and the San Antonio International Airport, according to the San Antonio Express-News , which was first to report on Waymo starting back up. Waymo told the paper that it has made changes to its software that will help the robotaxis better detect and avoid standing water in the future. items.t: Lucid Motors has a potential robotaxi partner for Europe
items.d: The company is partnering with mobility platform Bolt -- but no vehicle orders have been placed just yet.
items.fullText: Lucid Motors has entered into a partnership with European mobility platform Bolt that could bring robotaxis made by the California company to the continent. The two companies announced Thursday that Bolt “aims to deploy at least 25,000 fully autonomous vehicles” built on Lucid’s upcoming mid-size EV architecture, which is supposed to be smaller and cheaper than its current offerings. The announcement follows a major restructuring at Lucid Motors under its new CEO, Silvio Napoli, who recently laid off nearly 20% of the company’s workforce and delayed the launch of the first vehicle to be built on the mid-size platform by almost a year to the second half of 2027. Lucid Motors has yet to deploy a commercial robotaxi version of either of its two existing vehicles. The company has spent the last year working in partnership with Uber and autonomous vehicle firm Nuro to launch a robotaxi version of its Gravity SUV . That is supposed to happen by the end of 2026. Napoli has said he believes the business of becoming a robotaxi provider would have margins that “vastly” exceed those of “the traditional retail model.” Bolt intends to own and operate the fleet, according to a press release. The two companies “will work together from the product-development stage on an autonomous driving system (ADS)-ready vehicle platform,” it says. The vehicles will use Nvidia’s autonomous vehicle compute and sensing architecture (called Hyperion), but the companies did not say which company (or companies) will provide the autonomous driving software. Lucid declined to offer any more information beyond what was in the press release. No money has changed hands, and Bolt has not placed an order for the vehicles. items.fullText: Physical AI Takes the Wheel: How the World’s Robotaxi Leaders Are Building With NVIDIA Technologies NVIDIA’s modular, full-stack robotaxi pipeline — a three-computer solution spanning AI training, simulation and in-vehicle computing — is being adopted across the robotaxi ecosystem. September 10, 2026 by Ali Kani 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! The global robotaxi market — physical AI’s first commercial breakthrough — is projected to reach $400 billion by 2035 , with over 6 million commercial vehicles in operation as driverless fleets are already moving people through some of the world’s busiest and most complex streets. Deploying a driverless vehicle is one challenge. Scaling a fleet is a next-level computing challenge; it means delivering the same safe, reliable performance across thousands of vehicles. Meeting those demands requires enormous amounts of compute across the robotaxi development lifecycle, from preparing and training AI models to simulating and validating driving behavior, as well as real-time processing in the vehicle. NVIDIA provides an open platform for AI training , simulation and safety validation , with libraries, software development kits, workflows and models that developers can use alongside their own technology stacks. Every major robotaxi program operating at commercial scale today is running on NVIDIA’s modular stack, spanning AI training, simulation, in-vehicle computing — or a combination of the three — to develop and deploy fleets at scale. What Is a Robotaxi Technology Stack? A robotaxi technology stack is the end-to-end set of technologies used to develop, validate and deploy autonomous vehicles (AVs) — from data and AI model training to simulation, safety validation and real-time in-vehicle computing. NVIDIA’s robotaxi and AV platform brings these capabilities together in a three-computer solution: the model training computer, simulation and validation computer, and in-vehicle computer.
